### Details that will matter when coding

**C-mode middle alternates between two consumer inputs.** The observed sequences are:

```text
40 00 → 00 00
80 00 → 00 00
40 00 → 00 00
```

These represent Volume Increment, release, Volume Decrement, release, and so on. A remapper that listens only for Volume Up would miss alternating presses. [Raw capture](https://github.com/JPHutchins/ble-page-turner-investigations/blob/b21c12636439e1e705ad8c8e354253c0cae88980/captures/20261015T060407Z-eb800388708b.jsonl).

**Some physical controls are indistinguishable without knowing the switch position.** T-mode middle and C-mode upper produce byte-identical leftward gestures in these samples. Software cannot recover information that the packet stream does not distinguish. The client therefore needs explicit mode selection, calibration, or an honestly “unknown” mode state. [Captured sequences](https://github.com/JPHutchins/ble-page-turner-investigations/blob/b21c12636439e1e705ad8c8e354253c0cae88980/captures/20261015T061403Z-eb800388708b.jsonl), [corrected mapping](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870).

**The report-ID framing changes between APIs.** BLE notification values omit the report-ID prefix. Linux hidraw includes it for numbered reports. Apple CoreHID also includes it in `data` for multiple-report devices—even though it supplies an `id` argument separately. The handoff includes explicit normalization rules to prevent stripping or adding the ID twice. [Linux hidraw](https://docs.kernel.org/hid/hidraw.html), [Apple CoreHID notification contract](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/notification/inputreport(id:data:timestamp:)).

**The sample sends a coordinate outside its declared range.** One gesture reaches raw Y=1200 despite the descriptor declaring a maximum of 1000. The later OS event trace shows 1000. The decoder preserves that raw value; treating it as signed or dropping the gesture would be wrong. [Raw capture](https://github.com/JPHutchins/ble-page-turner-investigations/blob/b21c12636439e1e705ad8c8e354253c0cae88980/captures/20261015T061403Z-eb800388708b.jsonl), [OS event trace](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870).

The two capture files contain **237 notifications**, representing **25 touch gestures and six consumer-button presses**. They do **not** establish double-click, triple-click, long-hold, or chord behavior. I parsed those records and ran the handoff’s reference decoder against all 237 notifications successfully. The document provides a precise timing matrix for capturing the missing behaviors.

## 5. Your unrooted Fold6: Android 17 needs a specific capability check

Your screenshot matters here. **Android 17 has a new native HID API with Bluetooth support**, but “Android 17” alone does not establish that your installed build exposes everything needed.

The current official references document:

| Capability | Documented version |
|---|---|
| `HidManager`, enumeration, device opening, report descriptors | **37.1** |
| `HidDevice.registerEventListener()` and input-report callbacks | **37.2** |

These are minor API versions. The coding agent needs to check the installed build’s full SDK version and actual method availability. [HidManager](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/hardware/hid/HidManager), [HidDevice](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/hardware/hid/HidDevice), [37.2 API changes](https://developer.android.com/sdk/api_diff/37.2/changes/android.hardware.hid.HidDevice).

### There is also a real permission-documentation conflict

Google’s Android 17 enterprise overview calls `ACCESS_HID` a **dangerous-level permission**. The permission reference defines it as **`internal|appop`**. That prevents an honest promise that adding a manifest entry and showing a normal permission dialog will make raw HID work on your phone. [Enterprise overview](https://developer.android.com/work/versions/android-17), [permission reference](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/Manifest.permission#ACCESS_HID).

The handoff specifies a small diagnostic APK and no-root ADB checks to establish:

- Whether the classes and input-listener methods exist.
- How the phone actually defines `ACCESS_HID`.
- Whether the app can enumerate and open the F3.
- Whether it receives the touch and consumer reports.
- Whether native scrolling or volume changes still happen.
- Whether access survives backgrounding and reconnects.

### My practical prediction for your phone

**Foreground app-local handling is the strongest baseline.** The app can inspect the normalized key and motion events Android actually delivers to it. It does not automatically receive all original HID reports or events consumed by system policy. [Android InputDevice](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/InputDevice), [MotionEvent](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/MotionEvent).

**Global shortcuts from usable key events are plausible through a user-enabled AccessibilityService.** That could be useful for the C-mode middle button, subject to testing actual delivery and suppression. [Accessibility key filtering](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/accessibilityservice/AccessibilityService#onKeyEvent(android.view.KeyEvent)).

**Global interception of the touch gestures is substantially harder.** Android’s accessibility motion callback selects entire input-source types. Capturing `SOURCE_TOUCHSCREEN` can also withhold normal finger touches from the rest of the phone; filtering by device ID inside the callback does not transparently forward them again. The handoff therefore does not recommend that as the default solution. [Accessibility motion-event behavior](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/accessibilityservice/AccessibilityService#onMotionEvent(android.view.MotionEvent)).

**Receiving raw HID reports would still not prove exclusive control.** The new native HID API does not document an exclusive-grab operation. The agent must test whether the ring’s original gesture continues reaching other apps.

## Recommended starting point

**Start with the Linux read-only capture and decoder, while running the Fold6 capability probe in parallel.** Linux provides the clearest reference path through raw HID, translated input, and per-device input grabbing. macOS has native HID APIs with seizure support; Windows needs particular care because touchscreen collections have different access rules from consumer controls. [Linux hidraw](https://docs.kernel.org/hid/hidraw.html), [Apple CoreHID seizure](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/seizedevice()), [Windows HID access table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/hid/hid-architecture).

The file gives the coding agent the concrete protocol evidence, commands, decoder, platform restrictions, and acceptance criteria needed to proceed—and an explicit test for every material uncertainty.

I’ll check the Mac-versus-Linux differences, especially whether a custom app can take over the ring without its normal swipes or volume changes also happening.

**Yes—your understanding is mostly right, and I would build this for your Mac first.** We can share the code that understands the ring and decides what each press means, then have separate Mac and Linux code for receiving input and carrying out actions.

The qualification is that **we should test whether the Mac can take exclusive control of this particular ring early**, before building the rest of the app. Apple provides the necessary mechanisms, but we haven’t tested them with your physical unit. [Apple’s HID communication guide](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/communicatingwithhiddevices), [exclusive device access](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/seizedevice())

## What we’re actually programming

Think of the ring as sending small messages over Bluetooth. Those messages are called **reports**.

The awkward thing about this F3 is that a message doesn’t necessarily say “the top button was pressed.” In the published hardware tests, its buttons produce **simulated finger swipes or volume commands**. Our software recognizes those messages and assigns our own meaning to them. For example, in T mode, the middle button produces a leftward swipe; our app could interpret that as “toggle recording” instead. [Published F3 hardware test and button mappings](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)

There are three main pieces:

| Piece | What it does, in plain English | Can we share it between Mac and Linux? |
|---|---|---|
| **Input adapter** | Gets messages from the ring and puts them into a consistent format. | The interface can be shared; the underlying OS code differs. |
| **Ring decoder and mapping rules** | Recognizes the ring’s messages and decides “this means the middle button; run my recording action.” | **Yes. This is the main reusable part.** |
| **Action adapter** | Actually starts recording, changes tabs, runs a script, sends a keyboard shortcut, etc. | The action names can be shared; their implementations may differ. |

That division is a design recommendation. It means a future Linux version can reuse the ring knowledge without rediscovering every byte.

**We normally don’t need to write the Bluetooth connection machinery ourselves.** Mac and Linux already support HID—“Human Interface Device,” the general category used for things such as keyboards and mice—and expose received reports to applications. [Apple’s Bluetooth HID example](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/communicatingwithhiddevices), [Linux raw HID access](https://docs.kernel.org/hid/hidraw.html)

## What actually differs between Mac and Linux?

### 1. Both give us a route to the ring’s data

On Mac, Apple’s native HID APIs let an application find a Bluetooth input device and receive its reports. On Linux, the `hidraw` interface exposes raw HID reports, including reports from Bluetooth devices. These are different doors into substantially the same device information. [Apple HID communication](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/communicatingwithhiddevices), [Linux `hidraw`](https://docs.kernel.org/hid/hidraw.html)

**Having GNOME or a screen attached to the Raspberry Pi doesn’t change how the F3’s bytes should be decoded.** The desktop matters later, when deciding how to interact with applications. Assuming the Pi has working Bluetooth and the required Linux input interfaces, the shared decoder can be the same.

### 2. Reading a press and taking over a press are different jobs

Suppose you want the middle button to start recording. You probably don’t want it also sending its original swipe into whichever window is open.

Both platforms have mechanisms intended to let an application take exclusive control:

- **Mac:** Apple’s `seizeDevice()` attempts to make our application the device’s only active client.
- **Linux:** grabbing an input device with `EVIOCGRAB` prevents other input clients from receiving events from that device.

These mechanisms operate at different layers, so we must confirm that we have taken over every relevant part of the ring and that its original actions have stopped. **Simply reading its messages is not sufficient.** [Apple exclusive access](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/seizedevice()), [Linux input grabbing](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/libevdev/doc/latest/group__init.html)

This is the main reason I wouldn’t postpone *all* OS-specific work until the very end.

### 3. The permissions and action mechanisms differ

On Mac, expect to deal with **Input Monitoring** permission for observing input, and potentially **Accessibility** permission when controlling other applications through accessibility features. Those are user-granted permissions in System Settings. [Apple Input Monitoring](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/control-access-to-input-monitoring-on-mac-mchl4cedafb6/mac), [Apple Accessibility access](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/allow-accessibility-apps-to-access-your-mac-mh43185/mac)

Linux gives us direct input-device interfaces and can create a virtual keyboard or mouse using `uinput`, subject to the appropriate device permissions. That is one way a Linux version could turn a ring press into a normal keyboard shortcut. [Linux virtual input documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/input/uinput.html)

For either platform, I would prefer a target application’s supported command or API when available. Simulating a keyboard shortcut is another option. That choice belongs in the action adapter, separate from the ring decoder.

## How far does “code it however we want” go?

**Quite far for changing what your computer does in response to a press.** We can design our own mappings and software profiles: a media profile, a browsing profile, a recording profile, and so on. Those profiles don’t need to correspond to the ring’s physical T/C switch.

But there are two hardware limits to keep straight:

- **We can only distinguish information the ring actually sends.** In the published tests, T-mode middle and C-mode upper both produce the same leftward swipe. That signal alone cannot tell us which physical button/mode caused it. Keeping the switch in T and assigning its three distinct single-press gestures is a straightforward starting point. [F3 button mappings](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)
- **A complete single-press mapping doesn’t automatically establish hold behavior.** The published test describes short, synthesized swipe sequences. We still need measurements of holding and releasing the physical buttons before promising something like “record exactly while I hold this down.” A tap-to-toggle recording action does not have that same requirement. [F3 observed gesture behavior](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)

Also, changing the computer’s response does **not require changing the ring’s firmware**. Our research has not established a supported protocol for rewriting that firmware or remotely redefining its built-in modes.

## What I recommend next

**Start on the Mac, with a small proof of concept:**

1. Pair the ring and display the messages received from each button.
2. Attempt exclusive access and verify that unwanted native swipes or volume changes stop.
3. Connect the three T-mode single presses to three chosen actions.
4. Then investigate holds, double presses, reconnecting after sleep, and additional software profiles.

If those first two steps work, we have the foundation for a useful Mac application. Linux can remain an optional investigation tool and a later port.

So yes: **keep the ring decoder and mapping rules portable, and implement the OS connections separately—but prove the Mac can receive and take over the ring before investing in the full app.**

## T and C are two built-in button presets

For the F3’s **observed single presses**:

| Switch setting | What the ring sends | Intended use |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | All three buttons send simulated screen swipes: up, left, or down. | Scrolling videos and turning pages. |
| **C** | The outer buttons send left/right swipes. The middle button sends volume-key presses. | Page turning and camera control—a compatible camera app can interpret a volume-key press as “take a photo.” |

The physical-device tests document those signals; FiKavi’s camera guide describes the camera use. [F3 hardware tests](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870), [FiKavi camera guide](https://fikavi.com/f3-phone-camera-remote/)

So think of T and C as **two different button layouts programmed into the ring**. They don’t fundamentally change what we’re allowed to build.

## And yes, that’s exactly the Mac plan

Our app would:

1. **Receive the ring’s input messages.**
2. **Take exclusive control**, so those messages don’t also cause unwanted swipes or volume changes.
3. **Recognize which signal arrived.**
4. **Perform whatever action we assigned to it.**

Apple provides both report-reading APIs and an exclusive-access mechanism called `seizeDevice()`. **We still need to verify that takeover works properly with your F3.** [Apple input-report APIs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/communicatingwithhiddevices), [exclusive access](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/seizedevice())

For example:

> You press the middle button in T mode.  
> The ring sends its usual fake left-swipe gesture.  
> Our app recognizes it and toggles dictation.  
> Nothing needs to swipe on your screen.

One small terminology correction: we’re intercepting **the ring’s input reports**, not literally every low-level Bluetooth packet. macOS continues handling the Bluetooth connection.

**Once that interception works, understanding the ring and deciding what your Mac should do are separate problems.** We can leave the ring in T mode and give its three buttons entirely different purposes in our app.

[Apple’s ownership lifecycle](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/seizedevice())

## Why T rather than C?

**T was a small implementation convenience—not a claim that it is more reliable.** Your reasoning would make sense if C turned all three buttons into ordinary key presses, but **C still sends touch gestures for two of its three buttons**.

These are the observed single-press outputs:

| Button | T mode | C mode |
|---|---|---|
| Upper | Swipe up | Swipe left |
| Middle | Swipe left | Volume Up / Volume Down, alternating between presses |
| Lower | Swipe down | Swipe right |

[Published F3 hardware tests](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)

That gives us:

- **T:** one kind of decoder handles all three buttons—recognize three different swipe patterns.
- **C:** recognize two swipe patterns, plus handle volume-key messages. Treat either Volume Up or Volume Down as “middle button pressed.”

**That extra C-mode handling is straightforward. It isn’t a significant obstacle.**

Also, “touch gesture” sounds less deterministic than it actually is here. These are **short coordinate sequences generated by the ring’s firmware**, not someone physically dragging a finger at a slightly different angle each time. In the published test, repeated presses of each gesture-producing button sent identical coordinates. That supports their usefulness as recognizable signals, although it doesn’t establish reliability under every condition. [F3 repeatability observations](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)

### My actual recommendation

**Don’t commit to T on principle.** Capture both modes on your Mac, then choose based on what we observe.

For a **middle-button-only shortcut**, C is an attractive starting point because its volume-key message is simpler to interpret than a sequence of swipe coordinates. For **all three buttons**, T gives us a uniform format. Neither has a demonstrated overall reliability advantage from the evidence we have.

Once exclusive control works, **either mode can trigger the same custom Mac actions**. The mode mainly changes how our code recognizes the press—not what we can make that press do.

# chatgpt response

**Yes—Python is absolutely fine for this.** Receiving a few button reports, recognizing patterns, logging them, and triggering actions is a small workload. The fiddly part will be macOS device access and permissions, not Python’s speed.

I’d give your agent this direction:

## 1. Start with a Python HIDAPI binding

The common Python package is **`hidapi`**, usually imported as **`hid`**. It provides device enumeration and raw HID reads through the operating system. That’s the first route I’d try. Package names are confusing here: several Python bindings have similar names, so have the agent confirm which implementation it installed. [Python binding](https://github.com/trezor/cython-hidapi), [underlying HIDAPI project](https://github.com/libusb/hidapi)

**The important check is exclusive access.** Don’t assume “we opened it and can read reports” proves that macOS has stopped processing them. Have the agent check the binding’s Mac behavior and run our **take over → log only → verify no native effects** test.

If that binding makes exclusive access awkward, my fallback would be:

> A small Swift helper handles device ownership and reading. It streams JSON lines to Python. Python handles decoding, mappings, configuration, and actions.

That still leaves almost all the application in Python. Apple’s native HID APIs provide report notifications and explicit device seizure. [Apple HID guide](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/communicatingwithhiddevices), [device seizure](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corehid/hiddeviceclient/seizedevice())

**I wouldn’t start with Bleak just because the connection is Bluetooth.** For this first pass, use the HID interface macOS already provides. Bleak becomes relevant if you later investigate the ring’s additional BLE services.

## 2. Make the first version a really good recorder

Before implementing custom actions, record enough information that you can replay an experiment without touching the ring again.

For each received report, save:

- **A monotonic timestamp**, such as `time.monotonic_ns()`, for accurate intervals.
- **The original bytes**, preferably as hex.
- **The report ID and device/interface identity.**
- **Your experiment label:** physical switch position, button, single/double/hold, and trial number.

Use **JSONL**: one JSON object per line. Python’s standard `json`, `time`, and `logging` modules are plenty.

Keep the original bytes even after you add decoded fields. If the decoder is wrong, you can fix it and replay the recordings.

Two particularly useful traps to avoid:

- **One press can produce several reports.** Don’t trigger an action for every packet in a swipe.
- **Report-ID packaging differs between APIs.** Normalize it once at the input boundary; don’t blindly strip the first byte because an example did.

## 3. Test deliberately, with pauses between experiments

I’d test both T and C using this sequence:

1. Each button individually, several times.
2. Double and triple presses at different speeds.
3. Holds of roughly half a second, one second, and several seconds.
4. Release after each hold—does releasing produce anything identifiable?
5. Two-button combinations.
6. Mode changes, power cycles, and reconnects.

**Label the physical action independently of what the decoder thinks happened.** Otherwise the decoder can accidentally become its own “proof.”

For C’s middle button, test a sequence of successive presses, then repeat after reconnecting and power cycling. We already have evidence of alternating Volume Up/Down; the experiment should establish whether that alternation resets and whether holds behave differently. [Existing F3 observations](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)

## 4. Keep three things separate in the code

| Component | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Reader** | Own the device and deliver timestamped reports. |
| **Decoder** | Turn report sequences into named events, such as `middle_press`. |
| **Action handler** | Decide what `middle_press` should do in the current profile. |

Make the decoder accept recorded reports as well as live ones. That gives your agent a quick way to check changes against everything you’ve already captured.

For the action side, start with **a log message**, then a simple script or supported application command. Add simulated keyboard shortcuts only where useful.

**My strongest practical tip: get one clean, exclusive, logger-only session working before adding clever mappings.** Once that works and the recordings are labeled properly, the remaining work becomes ordinary Python event handling.

# chatgpt response

**Yes—that’s the core matrix: 2 modes × 3 buttons × 4 actions = 24 basic cases.** That should give us a solid **button-behavior spec for building our client**, with a few additions.

### 1. Your 24 cases

| Dimension | Values |
|---|---|
| Mode | T, C |
| Button | Upper, middle, lower |
| Action | Single press, double press, triple press, press-and-hold |

For each case, record **everything received from before the action until after release**, including the bytes and timing.

### 2. Timing is part of the experiment

“Double press” and “hold” aren’t completely specified until we test timing:

- **Double/triple:** try quick presses and more widely spaced presses.
- **Hold:** try a short hold and a longer hold; explicitly watch what happens **on release**.
- **Repeat:** run each case several times consecutively, then repeat relevant cases after reconnecting.

That last point matters because the published F3 tests observed C’s middle button alternating between Volume Up and Volume Down. One isolated press would miss that behavior. [F3 observations](https://github.com/JPHutchins/kindle-button-mapper-rs/pull/1#issuecomment-6205704870)

### 3. Mode changes are a separate transition test

You don’t need to multiply every button case by every connection scenario initially. Test these separately:

| Transition | What to check |
|---|---|
| **T → C and C → T while connected** | Does the connection drop? Do the device’s reported identity/capabilities change? Does switching itself send anything? Does our exclusive ownership survive? |
| **Power off → on in each mode** | Does it reconnect automatically? Does button behavior or any alternating state reset? |
| **Idle/wake and Mac sleep/wake** | Does the first press work, merely wake the ring, or get lost? Does our app regain ownership? |

If a transition changes the device’s state, then repeat the affected button cases in that state.

### 4. The result might say “the app must infer this”

For example, a double press might produce:

- A special, distinct “double press” message; **or**
- Two ordinary single-press sequences.

Both are useful findings. In the second case, **our Python code recognizes the double press from timing**. If we want single and double presses to perform different actions, we then have to choose how long to wait before deciding a press was only a single.

Likewise, a hold might produce repeated messages, a distinct message, or just the same initial message as a tap. Recording the release tells us whether true “do this while held” behavior is possible.

**So: your 24 cases + timing variations + transition checks = a very good practical spec.** Add simultaneous button combinations only if you want to support them; otherwise mark them untested.

The useful final record for each case is:

> **Starting state → physical action and timing → complete received sequence → resulting state → repeatability.**

That gives your agent enough to distinguish what the ring actually communicates from behavior we need to implement ourselves.

Its mostly bonus since doing so with one finger is kind of clumsy but what kind of things should be on lookout for ... like if clicking one button holding and then clicking another blocks second from being sent or send totally different second ?

---

# chatgpt response

**Exactly—both of those are possibilities.** Also watch for whether the **order, delay, and release order** change the result.

These are possibilities to investigate, not things we’ve established about your F3:

| What happens when you hold one button and press another | What that tells us |
|---|---|
| **Both send their usual messages** | The ring accepts overlapping presses. We still need to establish whether our app can tell they overlapped. |
| **The second button sends nothing** | Some kind of blocking or priority rule may exist. |
| **The second message arrives only after releasing the first** | The action may be queued or triggered by release. |
| **The second button interrupts the first button’s message sequence** | Our decoder must handle an unfinished gesture being replaced. |
| **The combination produces a different message** | There may be a distinct combination action we could map. |
| **Nothing unusual happens immediately, but later presses behave differently** | The combination may change some internal state or setting. |
| **Releasing either button produces another action** | Release behavior needs its own mapping—or filtering. |

## The biggest trap: does the computer actually know you’re holding it?

A physical hold **doesn’t necessarily remain visible in the messages**.

Compare these two experiments:

1. **Press and release upper**, wait one second, press middle.
2. **Press and hold upper**, wait one second, press middle.

**If the ring sends identical messages with identical timing in both experiments, our app cannot distinguish them.** We could recognize “upper, then middle,” but couldn’t reliably call it “hold upper as a modifier.”

That distinction matters if you imagine using one button like **Shift**, making the other buttons perform alternate actions. We need either a genuine, observable held/released state or a distinct combination message for that to work reliably.

## Also distinguish “blocked while held” from “temporarily busy”

Try pressing the second button:

- Almost immediately after the first.
- After holding the first for about a second.

If only the immediate second press disappears, the ring might be busy sending its first gesture or applying a short cooldown. If it disappears throughout the hold, that suggests a different rule. **The measurements establish the behavior; they won’t necessarily reveal the firmware’s reason.**

## A manageable test for each button pair

For **upper + middle**, for example:

1. Hold upper, tap middle, release upper.
2. Hold middle, tap upper, release middle.
3. Press both approximately together, then release upper before middle.
4. Repeat, releasing middle before upper.
5. Afterwards, tap each button normally to check that their behavior hasn’t changed.

Repeat for **middle + lower** and **upper + lower**, in T and C. You don’t need laboratory-perfect simultaneity: record that it was an attempted simultaneous press, and repeat it a few times.

**Even if combinations remain a bonus feature, this testing is useful:** it tells your agent how to handle accidental overlapping presses without misclassifying them as ordinary clicks. The first version can support the clear, repeatable patterns and leave ambiguous combinations unmapped.
